TRIBUTES TO MARTRYS SARDAR BHAGAT SINGH, RAJGURU AND SUKHDEV 
MR. CHAIRMAN:   Hon.  Members, today, the 23rd of March, marks the anniversary 
of the martyrdom of three of the most valia nt sons of Mother India — Sardar Bhagat 
Singhji, Rajguruji and Sukhdevji — who laid down their lives on this day in 1931 in the 
prime of their youth. Their unparalleled courage, indomitable spirit, and supreme 
sacrifice remain a shining ch apter in our recent struggle for freedom and continue to 
evoke deep respect and gratitude from every citizen of India. 
Hon. Members, their martyrdom was not merely an episode in the history of 
our Freedom Movement, it was a defining moment that awakened the conscience of 
the nation and inspired millions to rise in unity against colonial rule. The freedom that 
we cherish today is the result of the sacr ifice of countless patrio ts and, among them, 
this heroic trio occupies a special place in the heart of every Indian. 
On this solemn occasion, let us reaffirm our resolve to uphold the constitutional 
values and democratic principles for whic h these martyrs stood and to work unitedly 
for a strong, inclusive and progressive India. 
I request the hon. Members to rise in  their places and observe silence as a 
mark of respect to the immortal memory of Sardar Bhagat Singh ji, Rajguru ji and 
Sukhdevji. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.)

Statement 
(a)   Water and Sanitation is State su bject and Management of urban flooding 
falls under the purview of the State Go vernments and the Urban Local Bodies 
(ULBs)/Urban Development Authorities, who are responsible for maintaining the 
drainage and sewerage system. Government of India supplements the efforts of the 
States through schematic interventions/ advisories. It provides financial and technical 
support to the States to strengthen Urban Planning ecosystem.  
Usually, increased incidence of high intensity rainfall in short duration is mainly 
responsible for urban floods, which is fu rther compounded by unplanned growth, 
encroachment of natural water bodies, inadequate sewer systems, inadequate 
rainwater drainage systems, encroachments, etc.   
Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (A MRUT) launched in 
the year 2015, inter alia, has a component on storm water drainage, which involved 
construction and improvement of drains/ st orm water drains in order to reduce and 
eliminate flooding and creating green space s and parks. Under AMRUT, 838 Storm 
Water Drainage projects worth ₹3017.13 crore have been taken up and 3,798 water 
logging points have been eliminated so far. 
Further, 2,522 green spaces and park projects worth ₹1,604.13 crore have 
been taken up by the States/UTs under AMRUT and 5,286 acres of permeable green 
space area have been developed so far through these projects. 
Under AMRUT 2.0, projects for green sp aces and parks and rejuvenation of 
water bodies are taken up by the States. Under AMRUT 2.0, proposals of the States/ 
UTs for 2,991 water body rejuvenation projects worth ₹6,083.32 crorecovering around 
1,21,800 acres of area and 1,665 gr een spaces and park projects worth ₹1,103.71 
crore covering 13,893.82 acre, have been approved.  
Besides, under AMRUT and AMRUT 2.0 sewerage and septage management 
projects have been undertaken, which inter alia help in evacuation of storm water. 
Under AMRUT, as updated by State/UTs on AMRUT portal, 889 sewerage/septage 
management projects have been grounded, which has led to crea tion of 22,477 km 
length of sewer network. Under AMRUT 2.0, the State/UTs have taken up 584 
Sewerage and Septage Management projects covering 34,559 KM of sewer network.

Concern over protection and dignity of domestic workers 
DR. K. LAXMAN (Uttar Pradesh):   Sir, I draw the attention of Government to the 
condition of domestic workers -- one of the most vulnerable segments of India’s 
unorganized workforce. Domestic workers perform essential services such as 
cleaning, cooking, caregiving, and childcare,  supporting millions of households and 
enabling the functioning of urban economies. According to the E-Shram portal, about 
2.89 crore belong to the domestic and household workers category. A large 
proportion of them is women and migrants  from economically weaker backgrounds. 
Despite their important role, most domestic workers continue to work without written 
contracts, fixed wages, social security coverage or proper grievance redressal 
mechanisms. The Government has taken im portant steps to support unorganized 
workers through initiatives such as the E-Shram portal and the Code on Social

sectors. However, domestic workers face  unique challenges because their work 
takes place inside private homes, making regulation and protection difficult. Many 
remain vulnerable to irregular wages, long working hours, and sudden termination.  
I, therefore, urge the Government to consider recognizing domestic workers as 
‘essential service’ workers and to strengthen their inclusion in welfare programmes 
through better registration, access to so cial security, and effective grievance 
redressal mechanisms.  Such steps will help ensure dignit y, security, and fairness for 
millions of domestic workers as we move toward the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.

DR. FAUZIA KHAN (Maharashtra): Sir, I seek to draw attention of the Government to 
the precarious lives of India’s 7.7 million gi g and platform workers. This workforce, 
comprising our delivery riders and cab drivers,  is projected to grow to 23.5 million by 
2030. They are the visible pillars of ou r urban economy, yet they remain legally 
invisible. While the Code on Social Security, 2020, formally recognized these workers, 
they still lack an enforceable floor of prot ection. Independent reports indicate that 95 
per cent of these workers have no insura nce and 90 per cent have zero savings for 
emergencies. Most distressingly, workers face arbitrary deactivation where their 
livelihood is terminated overnight by an al gorithm without notice or a hearing. While 
States like Rajasthan and Karnataka have pi oneered welfare boards, a National Act is 
now essential to ensure uniform rights across State boundaries. I request for a 
solution-oriented approach based on three pillars. There is a need to establish a 
Welfare Fund, financed by a 2 per cent tr ansaction levy on aggregators to provide 
accident insurance and maternity benefits; granting workers the right to know, how 
they are scored and prohibiting ID blocking without human review; and, finally, setting 
up quasi-judicial authorities to resolve disp utes in a time-bound manner. Sir, I urge 
the Government to implement a comprehens ive national framework to protect the 
rights and livelihoods of gig workforce.

non-existent literally for the animals in our country.  The perpetrator's penalty is 
literally 100 times less than the victim's tr eatment cost. The Prevention of Cruelty to 
Animals Act, 1960, sets a maximum fine of Rs. 50 for first offence and Rs. 100 for 
subsequent ones.  These amounts, which were fixed over 65 years ago, have failed to 
deter cruelty while animal abuse cases continue  to rise nationwide.   Further, with the

enacted.  Meanwhile, global indices may place India in a moderate category, but

THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER A FFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC

Statement 
(a)  and (b)  Electronics and Information Technology Goods(Requirement of 
Compulsory Registration Order),2021 has been  notified by Ministry of Electronic and 
Information Technology (MeitY) through wh ich Electronics and IT products have 
been brought under compulsory BIS Registrati on as per provisions of Scheme- II of 
BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018. 
Under this Scheme, a licence to use or apply a Standard Mark, through 
registration based on self-declaration of co nformity, is granted for goods or articles, 
hereinafter referred to as products, ma nufactured in a manufacturing premises and 
conforming to all the requirements of the relevant Indian Standard(s). The 
manufacturer ensures that the product has b een tested for conformity against all the 
requirements of the Indian Standard and subm its test report which is issued by third 
party laboratory. 
At present, 65 product categories have been notified under the schedule of 
“Electronics and Information Technology Goods (Requirement of Compulsory 
Registration) Order, 2021 ”. The Order is equally applicable to imported or 
domestically manufactured goods. 
Earlier, as per Scheme-II of Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) Conformity 
Assessment (CA) Regulations, 2018, pr ovisions were available for Central 
Government to notify only Standard(s) fo r compulsory BIS certification. Now vide 
Gazette Notification dated 25th February,  2026 in the BIS Conformity Assessment 
Regulations, 2026, Scheme-II has been am ended to include provisions for Central 
Government to notify essential requir ements also besides Standard (s) for 
compulsory BIS certification.

renewal of Certification up to 5 years with  advance payment of fees for the entire 
renewal duration has been amended to allow annual payment of fee.

Expenditure (OOPE) of the patients visiting  the public health facilities, Government 
has rolled out the Free Drugs Service Initiative (FDSI) under National Health Mission 
(NHM). Under this, financial support is pr ovided to States / Union Territories for 
provision of free essential medicines in public health facilities based on the 
requirements posed by them in their Prog ramme Implementation Plans (PIPs) within 
their overall resource envelope. 
 
MoH and FW has recommended facility wi se Essential Medicines List (EML) 
including drugs for cancer treatment to be  made available at the public healthcare 
facilities: 
 
Sub Health Centre Health   Wellness Centre (SHC-HWCs) - 106 
Primary Health Centre Health and Wellness Centre (PHC-HWCs) - 172 
Community Health Centres (CHCs) - 300 
Sub-District Hospital - 318 
       District Hospital (DHs) – 381 
 
Support under the scheme is availa ble for Procurement of drugs and 
strengthening /setting up robust systems of procurement, Quality Assurance, Supply 
chain management and warehousing, Pres cription audit, gr ievance redressal, 
dissemination of Standard Treatment Guidelines and Establishment of IT enabled 
platform DVDMS (Drugs and Vaccine Distribution Management System) for

monitoring the real status of procuremen t and availability of essential medicines.To 
facilitate the monitoring of supply chain management activity at National level, a 
Central Dashboard has been de veloped. Few states have implemented the roll out of 
the DVDMS portal till Sub health centres wh ile many others are attempting to do so 
for the successful monitoring of the real status of procurement and availability of 
essential medicines. 
Furthermore, under the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana of 
Department of Pharmaceutical, Ministry of Ch emical and  Fertilizera total of 18,646 
Jan Aushadhi Kendras (JAKs) have been opened across the country as on 
28.02.2026,out of which 2,370, Jan Aushadhi Kendras has been openedspecifically in 
Government hospitalsto provide medicine s at rates that ar e about 50% to 80% 
cheaper than those of branded medicines. 
The product basket under the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojna 
has 2,110 medicines and 315 surgicals, me dical consumables and devices, covering 
all major therapeutic groups, such as cardiovascular, anti-cancer, anti-diabetic, anti-
infectives, anti-allergic and gastro-intestina l medicines and nutraceuticals. Almost all 
generic medicines included in the National  List of Essential Medicines, except lab 
reagents and vaccines, are part of the product basket. 
With a view to ensure accessibility and availability of medicines at JAKs, the 
following measures are in place: 
(i)     An end-to-end information-technology-enabled supply chain system 
consisting currently of five wareho uses and 41 distributors across the 
country, is in place. 
(ii) Since September 2024, stocking by Jan Aushadhi Kendras (JAKs) of 200 
commonly used medicines, consisting of the 100 top-selling medicines in 
the product basket and 100 fast-se lling medicines in the market, is 
incentivised with JAK owners being eligible to receive monthly incentive 
based on the stocks that they maintain of these medicines. 
(iii) In addition, with a view to ensure availability of commonly used products, 
400 fast-moving products are monitored regularly by the scheme 
implementing agency {Pharmaceutical s and Medical Devices Bureau of 
India (PMBI)} and demand for the same is forecasted on an ongoing basis. 
Further, steps have been taken to di gitise the forecasting method to 
augment the procurement process through automation.

Concern over operational and maintenance challenges faced by the               
UNESCO heritage, Darjeeling Himalayan Railway 
SHRI HARSH VARDHAN SHRINGLA (Nominated) :  Madam, I seek to draw attention 
to the need to preserve the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, popularly known as the Toy 
Train, a UNESCO World Heritage Site under the Mountain Railways of India. Built in 
1881, this engineering marvel connects New Jalpaiguri to Darjeeling across fragile 
Himalayan terrain.  For over 140 years, it ha s symbolized the region’s cultural identity 
and attracted tourists from India and abroad. However, serious operational and 
maintenance challenges now threaten its survival. Despite efforts by the Ministry of 
Railways, the railway corridor has gradua lly shrunk, compromising safety and 
efficiency. The line passes through land slide prone areas wh ere heavy rainfall 
frequently damages tracks and disrupts services, requiring constant monitoring and 
restoration. Ageing steam locomotives also demand specialised maintenance and 
custom built parts, necessitating sustained technical and financial support. The vision 
of “Vikaas bhi Viraasat bhi ” rightly emphasizes balancing development with heritage 
conservation. This Railway embodies that vision must be preserved through 
sustainable tourism and infrastructure strengthening. There is a need to enhance 
visibility through strategic marketing and to  develop an integrated tourism ecosystem 
linked with local culture and livelihoods. Ac tive participation of local communities, 
tourism stakeholders, and Self Help Groups can generate employment. Skill 
development of youth and railway staff in heritage conservation and modern 
maintenance is equally essential. 
I urge the Government to formulate a comprehensive conservation plan with 
adequate funding, infrastructure restor ation, corridor protection, and disaster

Concern on missing Indian Seafarers in International Waters 
DR. SASMIT PATRA (Odisha): Madam, I seek to highligh t the case of a young cadet 
from Odisha, who has gone missing in in ternational waters under unexplained 
circumstances. At the very beginning of his career, he boarde d a commercial vessel 
with aspirations of supporting his family and building a future. Instead, his sudden 
disappearance, after he was last seen on board has left his family in prolonged 
uncertainty, with no clear answers despite search efforts and limited transparency 
from authorities. This is not an isolated  incident. Official records reveal numerous 
Indian seafarers reported missing or dead under unclear conditions, with many cases 
still pending investigation years later. Thes e include incidents of explosions, onboard 
accidents, disappearances, and even alleged negligence by ship authorities. In one 
case, a cadet went missing mid-voyage  despite multiple onboard searches, 
highlighting serious gaps in monitori ng and accountability. Further, official 
communication indicates that nearly 50 Indian seafarers have died in a single foreign 
region since 2014, many of them between 18 and 24 years old. Several cases also 
point towards mental harassment, unsafe working environments, and delays in 
compensation and investigation. I, therefore, demand time-bound international probe 
into seafarers’ disappearance, mandatory r eal-time tracking and reporting of Indian 
crew on all vessels, a National Maritime Missing Persons Authority and a time-bound 
accountability for all pending cases.

OBITUARY REFERENCE   
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon'ble Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing away 
of Shriman Datta Meghe, a former Member of this House, on the 22nd of March, 2026, 
at the age of 89 years.  He served as the Member of the Rajya Sabha from April, 2002 
to April, 2008.  
 Born on the 11 th of November, 1936, at Paunar in Wardha district of 
Maharashtra, Shriman Datta Meghe started his legislative career as a Member of 
Maharashtra Legislative Assembly and se rved that Assembly for three terms. 
Shriman Datta Meghe also served as a Mini ster in the Government of Maharashtra 
holding several portfolios. He also served as a Member of the Lok Sabha for four 
terms. Shriman Datta Meghe made notable co ntributions in the fields of education 
and healthcare by establishing institutions that expanded access to higher education 
and medical services, particularly, for the under-privileged.    
In the passing away of Shriman Datta Meghe, the nation has lost an able 
parliamentarian, a veteran legislator and a dedicated social worker.  We deeply mourn 
the passing away of Shriman Datta Meghe.   
I request hon’ble Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark 
of respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon'ble Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
MR. CHAIRMAN : Secretary-General will convey to  the members of the bereaved 
family our sense of profound sorrow and deep sympathy. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: I request the entire House including the Ministers; when we are on 
Obituary Reference, we should maintain silence.  That is the way we should pay 
respect to the departed soul.

Need to identify and revive old water bodies in Delhi using historical maps 
DR. MEENAKSHI JAIN (Nominated) : Sir, the loss of our environmental heritage is a 
matter of growing concern. There is mounting awareness of the degradation of the 
ecology and the need to take remedial steps. The issue is : How do we reclaim our 
lost ecosystem? One possible answer can be  found in the study of old maps. They 
can help identify and locate water bodies, and then help in reclaiming parts of our lost 
heritage. I will give you one example. There is an old map of Delhi dated back to the 
year 1932. It shows a two-mile long water body spread across Kadipur and 
Naglipuna, that is, present day Kadipur. Google satellite imagery shows that large 
parts of the water body have been built upon. However, an almost 10 acre depression 
at the site suggests the possibility of some revival. There is also an opportunity for 
creating a biodiversity park which can help reduce adverse environmental impact in 
the area. If old maps can be used to trace lost water bodies in the Delhi region and 
the findings popularized, it will help creat e public awareness and sensitize people on 
the need to protect and possibly revive a great heritage. Such an study of the 
environmental legacy through old maps ca n be undertaken in many parts of the 
country to the benefit of our land. Thank you.

based census of our elephant population; initiatives aimed at protecting the Great 
Indian Bustard, Gharial and Sloth Bear, as well as the translocation of Cheetahs.  This 
is the “democratisation of technology ” in action, using data to bridge the divide 
between development and conservation.  I,  therefore, propose the following three 
initiatives: First, ‘Special Zones’ in our most sensitive corridors, within which wildlife-
sensitive engineering should be considered  as a mandate in the implementation of 
developmental projects.  Second, the creation of ‘Local Conservation Councils’ with 
the assistance of Biodiversity Manageme nt Committees and Gram Panchayats to 
institutionalise the role of our indigenous  communities in our in clusive conservation 
efforts.  Third, Gajraj AI-enabled intrusion detection system (IDS) installed in all trains 
that pass through elephant migration routes, especially in North Bengal and Assam.  
In the spirit of वसुधैव कुटुÇबकम, let us demonstrate to the world that India’s ‘Green 
Frontier’ is the global gold standard for a future where humanity and nature flourish 
together.  Ģकृित: रक्षित रिक्षता। धन्यवाद।

SHRIMATI REKHA SHARMA (Haryana) :  Hon’ble Chairman, Sir, I rise to highlight a 
critical issue regarding the effectiveness of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) 
initiatives in truly empowering women.  Today, CSR has become one of the most 
visible platforms for women’s empowermen t in India.  Annual reports showcase 
women attending training centres, entrep reneurship workshops, and leadership 
programmes. It creates an impression of progress.  But the ground reality is different.  
A large share of CSR spending is con centrated on short-term skill training 
programmes.   These often end with certi ficates, but not with jobs, income or 
sustainable livelihoods.  Training without market linkage, credit access, or institutional 
support has limited impact.  Even more co ncerning is that women are repeatedly 
channelled into traditional sectors tailori ng, handicrafts, beauty services where 
markets are already saturated and growth opportunities are limited.   
 Sir, the real issue is:  CSR programme s often prioritise what is visible and 
easily measurable, rather than what creates  lasting change.  Structural barriers like 
access to credit, integration into supply chains, procurement opportunities, and 
workplace reforms are rarely addressed because they are complex and require 
deeper commitment.   
 Sir, as a result, we are seeing a pattern  of visibility without viability and 
participation without power. Women are be ing trained to adjust within existing 
systems, instead of systems being re-designed to include women.  
Sir, I would like to suggest that CSR policies should encourage market-linked 
and outcome-based interventions, not just training numbers. Corporates must be 
incentivised to procure from women-led entrepreneurs and integrate them into supply 
chains. Greater focus is needed on credit access, digital inclusion, and formal market

(a) Ministry of Skill Development an d Entrepreneurship (MSDE) is 
implementing Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana 4.0 (PMKVY 4.0) since 2022, for 
imparting skill development training thro ugh Short-Term Training (STT) and up-
skilling and re-skilling through Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) to the youth 
across the country, including Haryana. The S ector-wise and district wise number of 
candidates trained under PMKVY 4.0, as on 31.12.2025, in the State of Haryana is

(b) Under PMKVY 4.0, various steps have been undertaken to introduce new-
age skill courses in order to keep pace with the evolving industry demands and advent 
of new age technologies. Over 600 industry -aligned courses have been introduced 
across emerging sectors such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), 5G technology, 
cybersecurity, green hydrogen, drone technol ogy, and logistics, with the objective of 
preparing the workforce for Industry 4.0. Trai ning is being imparted in future-ready 
job roles to meet the demands of emerging  sectors including drones, AI, robotics, 
and mechatronics. The courses offered und er PMKVY are designed by industry-led 
bodies to ensure relevance and responsi veness to the needs of these sectors. 
Further, District Skill Development Plans (D SDPs) are formulated by District Skill 
Committees (DSCs) to assess skill gaps and map industry demand at the district 
level. This ensures that PMKVY training programs remain closely aligned with local 
employment opportunities and regional workforce requirements. Additionally, 
emerging areas like green energy, semiconducto r, etc. have been prioritized in line 
with national missions and economic growth sectors. 
(c)  PMKVY 4.0 is a demand driven sche me, wherein training centres are 
accredited/ affiliated based on the proposal s submitted by the Project Implementing 
Agencies, after taking the skill gap into  account. Under the Scheme, training is 
delivered through various institutes of Ce ntral Ministries/Departments, PSUs, State 
Skill Development Missions, Industries, In dustry Associations, ITIs, Polytechnics, 
Higher Education Institutions, Training Providers, Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Kendras 
(PMKKs), etc. As on 31.12.2025, 668 tr aining centres have been accredited/ 
affiliated for imparting project based skilling in the State of Haryana.  
(d) The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) is actively 
collaborating with various Ministries/ Depa rtments to align skilling initiatives with 
national priorities and the specific skill requirements of different government schemes. 
This “Whole-of-Government” approach has enabled closer convergence of skilling 
efforts with industrial and economic priori ties across the country, including those of 
Haryana. The details are as under: 
i. M/o Micro, Small and  Medium En terprises for PM Vishwakarma: The scheme 
is jointly implemented by the Ministry of MSME, MSDE (nodal for skilling), and 
DFS, with a three-tier structure compri sing the National Steering Committee, 
State Monitoring Committees, and District Implementation Committees. The 
scheme covers 18 traditional trades, the scheme seeks to preserve skills while 
enhancing livelihoods, with a target to train 30 lakh artisans and craftsmen over

five years. As on 19 th March 2026, a total of 32,147 artisans have been trained 
in the State of Haryana. 
ii. M/o Women and Child Development (MWCD) for skilling adolescent girls: 
Under the NAVYA (Nurturing Aspirations through Vocational Training for Young 
Adolescent Girls) initiative, skilling of 3,850 adolescent girls (AGs) in non-
traditional job roles across 27 districts of 19 States has been targeted under the 
pilot phase. As on 19 th March 2026, a total of 34 Adolescent Girls have been 
trained in the State of Haryana. 
iii. M/o New and Renewable Energy fo r National Green Hydrogen Mission 
(NGHM): NGHM is one of the key flagship scheme of the Government aimed to 
create 6 lakh jobs. Skilling has been prioritized in geographies where plants 
under NGHM are being set up by industries. As on 19 th March 2026, a total of 
417 candidates have been trained in the State of Haryana. 
iv. M/o Electronics and Information Technolog y (MeitY) for India AI Mission and 
India Semiconductor Mission (ISM): This convergence aims to support India AI 
Mission through skilling in Artificial Intelligence (AI) related job roles under 
PMKVY 4.0 such as AI - Machine Learning Engineer, AI - Data Quality Analyst, 
AI - Database Administrator, etc. As on 19 th March 2026, a total of 1,037 
candidates have been trained in the St ate of Haryana. Moreover, under India 
Semiconductor Mission, as on 31 st December, 2025, a total of 13,941 
candidates have been trained across India. 
v. M/o Jal Shakti (M/oJS) for Nal Jal Mitra Programme under Jal Jeewan Mission: 
D/o Drinking Water and Sanitation in collaboration with MSDE has developed 
the Nal Jal Mitra Programme (NJMP) in  August 2023. NJMP envisages multi-
skilling of local people in rural areas, covering various essential skill sets, 
including Plumbing, Electrical work, Masonry, Pump Operations, and other 
allied skills. As on 19th March 2026, a total of 532 candidates have been trained 
in the State of Haryana. 
vi. Department of School Education and Literacy (D/oSEL) and Department of 
Higher Education (D/oHE): One of the key features of PMKVY 4.0 is alignment 
with NEP 2020 and cross utilization of available permanent infrastructure in 
higher Education Institutes (HEI) including Institutes of National Importance 
(INIs) / Universities / Colleges / Sch ools, etc. Skilling through education 
institutions have been increased under PMKVY 4.0 through the joint efforts of

Chakravyuha, Andha Yug,  Ritu - Samhara  and the Uttar Priyadarshi, etc., which 
brought immense glory to India on the global stage.  He was the first National School 
of Drama (NSD) graduate from Manipur, later serving as its Director from 1997 to 
1999 and as Chairman from 2013 to 2017. In 1976, he founded the ‘Chorus Repertory 
Theatre’ in Imphal, which became  a nationally-acclaimed centre of experimental and 
socially-conscious theatre.  
His contributions were recognized with Padma Shri, Sangeet Natak Akademi 
Award and Sangeet Natak Akademi Fellowship, among many other honours. In 
recognition of his extraordina ry contribution in theatre, he was conferred the ‘Legend 
of India -- Lifetime Achievement Award’ in 2018 by the then Vice -President of India, 
Shri M. Venkaiah Naidu.   Shri Ratan Thiyam elevated Manipuri theatre to national and 
international prominence and became a symbol of India's cultural depth, diversity and 
artistic excellence. I, therefore, urge the Government of India to confer Bharat Ratna 
posthumously upon Shri Ratan Thiyam as a fitting tribute to a legendary son of 
Manipur and one of the greatest cultural ambassadors of India. Thank you, Sir.

Statement 
(a) to (f) Regular inspections, demarcations and periodical verification of the 
railway land boundaries are carried out by railway administration and accordingly land 
records are updated. 
Indian Railway works closely with state revenue authorities to ensure 
continuous verification and updation of land records wherever required.

land, out of which about 0.21% (1068 ha) of Railway land is under encroachment. 
Regular field surveys are carried out by railways and necessary action is taken 
to remove the encroachment with the assistance of state governments. 
During the last five years, about 98.02 Ha of railway land has been reclaimed 
from encroachments.

FARMERS WELFARE be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether Government has formulated any plans to increase the area under 
millet cultivation in Punjab as part of efforts to diversify cropping patterns 
and reduce dependency on water-intensive crops like paddy; 
(b)  the steps being taken to ensure the availability of high -yield and drought -
resistant millet seeds to farmers in Punjab and the extent of distribution, in 
the last three years; and 
(c)  whether Government is promoting value -added products of millet in Punjab

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE (SHRI SHIVRAJ 
SINGH CHOUHAN): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c)   The Department of Agriculture  and   Farmers Welfare (DA and FW) 
is implementing various schemes to promote Crop diversification including the 
National Food Security  and  Nutrition Mission (NFSNM) under which, Millet (Shree 
Anna) cultivation is promoted. Interventions under NFSNM are being  implemented 
across 28 States and 2 Union Territories (UTs) including Punjab, for enhancing the 
production of various crops including Millets (Shree Anna) through area expansion 
and productivity improvement. Under NFSNM, for the financial year 2025 -26, an 
Annual Action Plan of Rs. 34.60 lakhs (Central share +state share) was approved for 
the state of Punjab to promote Millet cultivationin the state. The Approved Plan for 
NFSNM -Shree Anna includes assistance to the farmers through the state for 
demonstration, seed distribution, seed production, INM and IPM distribution,  
training etc.

Further, the Crop Diversification Programme (CDP) under the Pradhan Mantri - 
Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (PM -RKVY) is also being implemented in the Original 
Green Revolution States viz; Haryana, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh since 2013 -14 to 
divert the area of water guzzling paddy crop to alternative crops like millets, pulses, 
oilseeds, coarse cereals etc. In 2025 -26, an Annual Action Plan of Rs. 103.75cr 
(central share + state sh are) has been approved for the state of Punjab for various 
interventions supportingcrop diversification from Paddy to other alternative crops. 
 The Indian Council of Agriculture Researchensures the production of Breeder 
Seeds of new varieties/hybrids of mi llets. A total of 110 varieties of millets have been 
released during the last three years. High -yielding, climate -resilient, bio -fortified 
varieties or hybrids that are resistant to insects, pests and diseases, as well as of 
short and medium duration (less  than 10 years old) that  outperform existing 
prominent varieties are promoted under NFSNM. In Punjab, a total of 140 quintals of 
certified seed of millets have been distributed under the scheme duringfinancial year 
2025-26.  
The Government has been taking various initiatives to promote millet 
cultivation, processing and consumption across the country alongwith incentivizing 
food processing units, and exporters engaged in millet -based products. The Ministry 
of Food Processing Industries (MoFPI) is implementi ng the Production Linked 
Incentive Scheme for the Food Processing Industry (PLISFPI) from 2021 -22 to 2026-
27 and one component of the scheme focuses on Millet -Based Products, with an 
outlay of Rs. 800 crores (PLISMBP). Under the scheme, 29 applicants have been 
incentivized with an amount of Rs. 793.27 crore in the country including three projects 
in Kapurthala, Patiala and Jalandhar districts of Punjab. 
 Further, under the Pradhan MantriFormalisation of Micro Food Processing 
Enterprises (PMFME) Scheme, Mill ets and millet -based products have been 
identified as One District One Product (ODOP) in 21 districts of 11 States and 17 
Incubation Centers have been approved in 10 States having Millet processing lines. 
Under PMFME, 4,612micro food processing enterprises  have been approved with

Integration of digital land records with agricultural schemes 
*364. SHRIMATI SULATA DEO: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
[ 27 March, 2026 ]
69

(a)  whether the Ministry proposes to introduce integration of digital land records 
with agricultural schemes in Odisha to ensure transparency in Direct Benefit 
Transfer (DBT); and 
(b)  if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE (SHRI SHIVRAJ 
SINGH CHOUHAN): (a) and (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
 (a) and (b) Yes, Odisha is utilizing digital land records of farmers for the 
purpose of Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) under various agricultural schemes.  Odisha 
has operationalized the integration of digital land records, i.e., the Bhulekh database, 
with agricultural schemes in the State. The land records in the State are digitized and 
maintained by the Revenue and Disaster Management Department, Govt. of Odisha, 
in the Bhulekh portal. 
The State of Odisha has informed that the digitized land record database of the 
State is used for identification of landholding categories (such as small and marginal 
farmers) under the State Sector farmers’ welfare scheme, i.e. CM KISAN.  
Further, the State Farmers Registry under AgriStack, built using the Record of 
Rights in the sta te of Odisha covers landholding farmers, livestock and fisheries 
farmer, and provides them with a digital identity, called Farmer ID. It has been 
designed to integrate and validate farmer -related data. This helps enable accurate 
identification of eligible beneficiaries and helps enable Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) 
to the farmers with enhanced transparency, and efficient delivery of scheme benefits. 
Odisha has linked the AgriStack to register new farmers under the PM KISAN 
scheme. 
Under both CM KISAN and PM  KISAN schemes, financial assistance is 
transferred directly to the bank accounts of eligible farmers through DBT mode. 
 The State also captures digitized land record information at the time of farmer 
registration / Krushak Odisha (the State’s own farmer database) at the time of farmer 
registration. These records are subsequently used for DBT of various benefits, 
including seed input subsidy and need -based input assistance, to the farmers across 
the State.During the release of 22nd installment of PM Kisan i n Odisha, 34,18,193 
beneficiaries received benefit of scheme amounting to 683.64 cr. The total amount 
70
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

disbursed till date through DBT for the farmers in Odisha under PM -KISAN is 
Rs.14,486.34 crores. 
Further, the Digital Crop Survey, i.e., survey to digital ly capture crops being 
grown on every farmland in the country with photos and geo -tags, has enabled plot-
level visibility of crops and better estimation of areas sown across seasons, which in 
turn supports evidence-based planning for production estimation, procurement, input 
supply and logistics management. In Kharif 2025, the Digital Crop Survey (DCS) has 
been conducted in 604 Districts covering more than 28.5 crores plots, including 2.56 
crores plots in Odisha.

Need to strengthen the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) 
SHRI NIRANJAN BISHI (Odisha) : Mr. Vice -Chairman, Sir, I seek to draw the 
attention of the Government towards the functioning of the National Commission for 
Scheduled Tribes (NCST), a vital constitutional body entrusted with safeguarding the 
rights and interests of our tribal communities. The NCST has been established under 
Article 338A of the C onstitution of India, with the mandate to investigate, monitor and 
evaluate all matters relating to the safeguards provided for the Scheduled Tribes. The 
Commission is vested with the powers of a Civil Court in matters of inquiry, including 
summoning witne sses, requisitioning documents, and receiving evidence on 
affidavits. As of late 2023 and early 2024, four out of five key constitutional positions in 
the NCST remain vacant — including the Chairperson (vacant since 27 June 2023), 
the Vice -Chairperson (vac ant since 2019), and two Member positions. This has 
severely affected the decision -making capacity and institutional effectiveness of the 
Commission. Further, out of a total sanctioned strength of 124 posts, over  70 
positions remain vacant, including critical posts such as Directors, Research Officers, 
Law Officers, Accounts Officers, and Superintendent of Police. The Commission is 
functioning at less than 50 per cent capacity, significantly hampering its ability to 
conduct investigations, address grievances, and ensure justice for Scheduled Tribes. 
Therefore, I urge the Government to take necessary steps to fill all vacant positions, 
strengthen institutional capacity, and empower the NCST to effectively discharge its 
constitutional responsibilities across the country.

fantastic work for poor people of this co untry and he was the greatest Buddhist that 
India has ever seen. He is th e shining star in Indian history. But, nobody knew what 
his real name was. In 1915, a British offi cer by the name of Cecil Beadon came to a 
sleepy village known as Maski in  Raichur district in Karnataka. There, he saw a stone 
inscription on a hill and he said, “Here is Ashoka who is known as Devanampiyadasi 
Ashoka.” From that day onwards to this day,  we know the greatness of Ashoka. His 
name is everywhere in the world. The second  example I want to give you is about Gir 
Hill. If you go to Girnar Hill, on the right side, there are three insc riptions. One of them 
is by Ashoka, which explains how a king should behave and how people should be 
kept happy. Second is from the Gupta Dynasty, describing how they conquered 
India. The third is of Raja Rudradaman, who repaired a lake at his own expense 
without imposing any taxes.  Actually, all the stone in scriptions are not just 
inscriptions; they are the chain between the past and the present. If there are no 
stone inscriptions, we will never ever know  what it was 1,000 years back or 1,500 
years back. Actually, when you look at the statistics, 80 per cent of stone inscriptions 
date back 1,000 years. The stone inscriptions shared major information and later 
materials like paper, bhoja patra , tada patra , etc., came into use. So, stone 
inscriptions play an important role in our co untry's culture and history. Sir, in my work 
I have seen, -- this is my passion -- the stone inscriptions have become a stepping 
stone in some villages or a washing st one in some riverbeds. Once they are 
destroyed, we cannot get them back. I want  to congratulate our Government, which, 
in 2025 and 2026, instituted a new mission  known as Gyan Bharatam that actually 
collects all the manuscripts all over India. Rs. 491 crore has been assigned for this 
work for the period of five years, so that  we can save our manuscripts. If we do not 
know history, our past, we will not know ou r future. If one wants to be confident in 
our country, one should know the roots of our country, that is, our history. So, I 
request the Government of India to instit ute another mission, where we can save all 
our stone inscriptions, whether on gold, on copper plate or on stone, using the latest 
method of digitization.

SHRI SUKHENDU SEKHAR RAY (West Bengal) : Hon’ble Chairman, Sir, Article 
19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution guar antees the Right to Freedom of Speech and 
Expression to all citizens, including studen ts, faculty and researchers in Universities. 
Higher Educational Institutions in our country  have historically been spaces for vibrant 
intellectual debate, where diverse political , social and cultural ideas are openly 
discussed. This environment plays a crucial role in nurturing critical thinking and 
active citizenship among young people. However, in recent years, the exercise of free 
expression on campuses has faced several challenges. In the 2025 update, in the 
Academic Freedom Index, India ranked at 156 out of 179 countries assessed in the 
Report. Instances of campus protests, re strictions on student gatherings and 
disciplinary actions against dissenting voic es have raised con cerns about shrinking 
spaces for dialogue. Universities encour age debates, seminars and student-led 
discussions without fear of censorship or  retaliation. Strengthening institutional 
autonomy and reducing undue political in terference are also essential steps in 
maintaining academic independence. Ultimately , preserving freedom of expression in 
Indian Universities requires a collectiv e effort from administrators a nd the 
Government.  
Sir, the Fundamental Duties of the citize ns mandated under Article 51A of the 
Constitution stipulates, “ It shall be the duty of every citizen to develop scientific 
temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform. ” This balance is vital for

from Govt. of Telangana during the last three years. 
 Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) scheme, being implemented by Department of

March, 2022 and now being implemented und er Pradhan Mantri - Rashtriya Krishi 
Vikash Yojna (PM-RKVY). PDMC scheme focuses on enhancing water use efficiency 
at the farm level through micro-irrigation techniques, namely drip and sprinkler 
systems. Total central assistance of Rs. 873.95 Crore has been provided to 
Telangana under PDMC, out of which, Rs. 194.63 Crore provided during the last three 
years.

Need for installation of more Doppler Weather Radars in the North-East Region 
SHRI MAHARAJA SANAJAOBA LEISHEMBA (Manipur) : Sir, due to its complex 
mountainous terrain, heavy monsoon rainfall, frequent flash floods, landslides, 
thunderstorms, cloudbursts and increasing climate induced extreme weather events, 
the North-East region requires a far strong er and denser weather monitoring system 
than what presently exists. Here are some  reasons for additional Doppler Weather 
Radars (DWRs) in the region. Firstly, improved forecasting and early warning -- 
Doppler Radars can accurately track precipi tation patterns, detect thunderstorms, 
and provide early warnings for floods, landslides, and cyclones. Second is, 
strengthening Disaster Management.  With better weather forecasting, authorities can 
evacuate people, prepare emergency services, and minimize damage to 
infrastructure and agriculture. Third is, agricultural benefits. Accurate weather 
forecasts can help farmers to plan their acti vities, reducing crop losses and improving 
yields. Fourth is, flood and landslide risk reduction. North East India is prone to 
floods, and Doppler Radars can help mo nitor rainfall patterns, enabling timely 
interventions. Fifth is, climate change mi tigation. As climate change increases 
extreme weather events, Doppler Radars can help to monitor and predict these 
changes. 
 Currently, there are limited Doppler Rada r installations in the North East. In 
Assam, these radars are installed at Guwa hati, Dhubri, Jorhat, Tezpur, and Silchar. 
In Mizoram at Aizawl, in Nagaland at Dimapur, in Manipur at Imphal, and in Arunachal 
Pradesh at Mandala Top and Namsai. Adding  more DWRs can significantly improve 
weather forecasting and disaster management in the region. I, therefore, urge the 
Government to set up more Doppler Weather Radars in the North East Region.

Demand for strict implementation of the Supreme Court guidelines for  
the cancellation of fake caste certificates 
SHRI NIRANJAN BISHI (Odisha) : Sir, I seek to draw attention of the Government to 
the serious injustice faced by genuine Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes due to 
the misuse of fake caste certificates by inel igible persons. Despite clear directions of 
the hon’ble Supreme Court of India rega rding verification and cancellation of 
fraudulent caste certificates, many non-SC /ST individuals continue to obtain such 
certificates and illegally avail benefits mean t exclusively for the most marginalized 
communities. As a result of which, they secure Government jobs under reserved 
quotas, obtain admission to professional courses such as MBBS and Engineering, 
purchase protected SC/ST land, and recei ve scholarships, subsidies and other 
welfare benefits meant for genuine beneficiaries. This directly violates the 
constitutional safeguards provided under Articles 15(4), 16(4), 46, 338 and 338A of 
the Constitution of India, which mand ate the protection and advancement of 
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

benefits for years. Therefore, I urge the Government to ensure time-bound disposal of

constitutional duty and a moral responsibility of the State. Thank you, Sir.

SHRI SANT BALBIR SINGH (Punjab) : & Hon’ble Chairman Sir, I thank you for giving 
me this opportunity. Sat Sri Akal to all th e Hon’ble Members present in this House. 
Sir, in our country, doctors have traditionally been accorded the status of God, and 
medical services have always been regard ed as sacred. However, it is deeply 
concerning that healthcare today is increasingly being commercialized and treated as 
a profit-making enterprise. Private hospitals have become prohibitively expensive and 
are beyond the reach of the common man. At the same time, insurance companies 
lure citizens into purchasing policies through tall claims and assurances of 
comprehensive support during medical em ergencies—moments when individuals are 
most vulnerable and in need of care. However, when claims are actually made, 
patients are often denied benefits on the basis of complex, technical, and fine-print 
terms and conditions. These clauses are de liberately drafted in a manner that is 
difficult for an ordinary person to understan d, resulting in exploitation and financial 
distress for consumers. Sir, I urge the Government to take immediate steps to 
regulate both private hospitals and insura nce companies, and to put an end to the 
exploitation of the common ma n. There is an urgent need to plug systemic loopholes 
and ensure transparency and accountability in this sector. Further, I strongly 
recommend that all policy terms and conditio ns must be written in simple language, 
preferably in the mother to ngue of the consumer, so that individuals can fully 
understand their rights and obligations and protect themselves from unfair practices. 
Sir, today, patients are increasingly being treated as mere commodities for profit, with 
private hospitals and insurance companies often acting in collusion, thereby 
compromising access to quality and a ffordable healthcare. Due to such 
circumstances, patients from nearly eight st ates are compelled to seek treatment at 
PGI Chandigarh, leading to excessive burden on the institution and immense hardship 
for patients and their families. Therefore,  I demand that another super-specialty 
hospital be established in this region of Punjab to reduce the load on PGI and improve 
accessibility to quality healthcare. It is the responsibility of the Government to ensure 
adequate medical infrastructure for its ci tizens. At the same time, I would like to 
inform this august House with a sense of pr ide that Punjab has become the first state 
to provide free medical treatment up to ₹10 lakh through empanelled hospitals. I urge 
that such a progressive scheme be replicated across other states for the benefit of the 
wider population. Thank you, Sir.

Statement 
 (a) and (b)  The Government has launched Pradhan Mantri Skilling and 
Employability Transformation through Up graded ITIs (PM-SETU) scheme for the 
infrastructure upgradation of Industrial Tr aining Institutes (ITIs) across the country 
including the State of Uttar Pradesh. The scheme envisages to enhance the overall 
quality and relevance of vocational traini ng with upgraded labs, machines, and 
industry-aligned curriculum in the country. The Scheme has a total outlay of Rs. 
60,000 crores (Central Share – Rs. 30,00 0 crore, State Share – Rs. 20,000 crore 
and Industry Share – Rs. 10,000 crore). 
The key objectives of the scheme are: 
i. To improve the quality of training delivery in ITIs and National Skill Training      
 Institutes (NSTIs); 
ii. To modernize infrastructure and equipment as per industry standards; 
iii.  To introduce industry-aligned long-term and short-term courses, especially 
 in new and emerging sectors; 
iv.  To strengthen industry linkage for demand-driven skilling and better 
 employment outcomes; and 
v. To enhance the capacity of National Skill Training Institutes (NSTIs) for  
 training of trainers. 
The scheme comprises of two components: 
Component I – Upgradation of 1,000 Government ITIs (200 Hub ITIs and 800 
Spoke ITIs) in a Hub and Spoke model wherein upgradation includes smart 
classrooms, modern labs, digital content, and new courses aligned to industry 
needs. 
Component II – Capacity Augmentation of five NSTIs located in Bhubaneswar, 
Chennai, Hyderabad, Kanpur, and Ludhiana, including setting-up sector-
specific National Centres of Excellence for skilling, with focus on advanced 
training of trainers with global partnership.

Under the PM-SETU scheme, industry pa rticipation in curriculum design, 
training delivery and apprenticeship opportunities is strengthened through an 
industry-led governance model. The indust ry-led Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) is 
provided the necessary autonomy to prop ose modifications in the curriculum by 
introducing new courses and upgrading existing courses as per industry 
requirements. The scheme focuses on im proving employability outcomes through 
industry-led governance and aims to enable  learners to acquire industry-relevant 
skills, gain exposure to real work environments, and access career guidance, 
placement support and self-employment opportunities through strengthened 
institutional systems and industry linkages. 
Upgradation of curricula for ITI training programmes is a continuous process 
and is generally undertaken every three ye ars. To meet the demands of the modern 
economy and emerging technologies in the industrial sector, new courses are 
continuously developed and existing cour ses are upgraded in consultation with 
industry, academia and States/UTs. The courses are updated by incorporating new 
technologies and the latest tools, equipm ent and machinery in the curricula, keeping 
in view the requirements of emerging technologies. During the last three years, 14 
Craftsmen Training Scheme (CTS) courses, 15 short-term courses and 07 Flexi-MoU 
courses have been develo ped and approved by National Council for Vocational 
Education and Training (NCVET). Addition ally, 22 courses have been revised and 
approved to further align training with in dustry requirements. The list is attached at 
Annexure-I. 
Under CTS, 31 New Age Courses, in cluding Green Hydrogen Production 
Technician and Internet of Things Technician, have been intr oduced in ITIs. The 
enrolment of trainees in ITIs across the country in the New Age Courses has increased 
from 8,611 in session 2022-23 to 42,338 in session 2025-26. The list of these 31 New 
Age Courses is at Annexure-II. 
 (c)  Release of funds under PM- SETU for Upgradation of ITIs  is contingent

Statement 
 (a) The Ministry of women and Child De velopment is the nodal Ministry for the 
administration of Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ 
Act, 2015) which is the primary legislation for ensuring safety, security, dignity and 
well-being of children and is implemented by all the States an d UTs including the 
State of Uttarakhand. The Act creates statutory structures at the State and District 
levels which include State Child Protection Society (SCPS), State Adoption Resource 
Agency (SARA), Child Welfare Committees (CWCs), Juvenile Justice Boards 
(JJBs), District Child Protection Units (DCPUs ). It also provides for establishment of 
Child Care Institutions (CCIs). 
Under the JJ Act 2015 (Sections 27-30), the Child Welfare Committees 
(CWCs) have been empowered to take decisi ons with regard to the children in need 
of care and protection, keeping their best inte rest in mind. They are also mandated to 
monitor the function of the Child Care Inst itutions (CCIs). As per Section 106 of the 
JJ Act 2015, the primary responsibility for the implementation of the Act lies with 
the State Governments and Union Territory (UT) Administrations. At the national and 
state level, the JJ Act provides the Nati onal/State Commissions for Protection of 
Child Rights to monitor the implementation of the Act (Section 109). 
Inspection Committees are mandated under section 54 of JJ Act, 2015 to visit 
such facilities housing children. District Magist rate is the nodal authority in the district 
for children in need of  care and protection and to take action on the findings of the 
report submitted by the Inspection Committees. The Ministry regularly follows up with 
the State and Union Territory Governments and various advisories have been issued 
so as to ensure the effective implementation of Mission Vatsalya Scheme. 
The Ministry regularly follows up wi th the State and Union Territory 
Governments and various advisories have been  issued so as to ensure the effective 
implementation of Mission Vatsalya Scheme. 
 (b) and (c) The Ministry of Women and Child Development is implementing a 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme, namely ‘Mission Vatsalya’, through the State and UT 
Governments to deliver various services for Children in Need of Care and Protection 
(CNCP) as well as Children in Conflict wi th Law (CCL). These services include 
Institutional Care and Non-Institutional Care.  The Child Care Institutions (CCIs) 
established under the Mission Vatsalya sc heme support, inter-alia, age-appropriate 
education, access to vocational training, recreation, health care, counselling

etc. Under non-institutional care, support is provided to the children through 
Sponsorship, Foster Care, Adoption and After Care. 
As per Mission Vatsalya Guidelines, a CCI having capacity of 50 children can 
have Special Unit for 10 children with sp ecial needs. Similarl y, a CCI having the 
capacity of 25 children can have Special Unit for 5 children. 
The scheme provides for Special Educat ors/therapist and Nurse required for 
such children in CCIs. The Scheme also pr ovides the institutions, inter-alia, with 
specialized equipment and materials like Ps ychological test materials, training 
materials for speech and language, teachi ng materials, wheel chairs. CCIs under 
Mission Vatsalya also provide counselling and psychological support services as a 
standard component of care. Rehabilitation frameworks include individual care plans, 
health services, and emotional support mechanisms. 
The Ministry of Women and Child Deve lopment in collaboration with Lal 
Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Ad ministration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie has 
developed an online training module on Ju venile Justice (Care and Protection for 
Children) Act, 2015 for capacity building of  multiple stakeholders such as State 
Governments and UT Administrations, district  authorities and others. Various training 
and capacity building programmes have been conducted for child protection 
functionaries and other stakeholders across the States and UTs. 
 (d)    Section 41 of the JJ Act, 2015 mandat es every institution which is meant, 
either wholly or partially, for housing ch ildren in need of care and protection or 
children in conflict with law, to be register ed under the Act. The act further provides 
State Governments the power to grant and cancel registration of Child Care 
Institutions which provide rehabilitation an d reintegration services as specified in 
section 53 of the Act. 
 (e)   Mission Vatsalya promotes family ba sed non-institutional care of children 
in difficult circumstances based on the princi ple of institutionalization of children as a 
measure of last resort. Unde r non-institutional care, support is provided to the 
children through Sponsorship, Foster Care , Adoption and After Care. The scheme 
provides Rs.4000/- per month to children  eligible for non-institutional care 
(Sponsorship/ Foster Care/ Aftercare) on cost sharing basis. 
The Ministry has also issued Model Fost er Care Guidelines, 2024 to ensure 
clarity, efficiency and compliance amongst the stakeholders.

incarcerated parents remain among the most invisible groups in India’s justice 
system. Despite their vulnerability, there is  no reliable national data on how many 
such children exist, their liv ing conditions, or their acce ss to education and welfare. 
Even within prisons, ba sic facilities such as cr èches and childcare support are either 
inadequate or absent, while children outside face stigma, disruption in schooling, and 
economic distress. According to the Nati onal Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), the 
study notes that as of December 2023, a to tal of 1,492 children were living inside 
Indian prisons, with 1,318 women. Since prisons and law and justice fall under the 
State List, there is no uniform national fr amework, no standardised data collection, 
and no minimum benchmarks of care for these children. As a result, States follow 
fragmented approaches, and these children re main outside the focus of both justice 
and welfare systems. Prison data in India does not capture the long-term impact on 
children, nor does it track outcomes post-i ncarceration. The absence of data itself 
reflects the absence of policy attention. 
I urge the Government to develop a uniform policy framework with minimum 
standards of care. Additionally, establis h a national database of children of 
incarcerated parents, and ensure coordi nation between prison administration, 
education systems, and child protection servi ces so that these children are not left 
behind. Thank you so much, Sir.

Demand for creation of an independent Postal Circle for Goa 
SHRI SADANAND MHALU SHET TANAVADE (Goa) : Sir, I seek to draw attention of 
the Government to a serious administrative issue concerning postal administration in 
Goa. At present, postal services in Go a are administered under the Maharashtra 
Postal Circle. Despite being a separate State with its own distinct identity, Goa 
continues to remain under the administrative control of this circle. While this 
arrangement may have been suitable earlier , it no longer meets present needs, as 
Goa has its own administrative, linguistic and socio-economic requirements. This 
continued dependence on another State’s ad ministrative structure has led to several 
practical challenges. Firstly, recruitment to postal services is conducted at the circle 
level. As a result, candidates from larger  States tend to dominate the selection 
process due to greater competition, thereby limiting fair employment opportunities for 
164
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
 
local youth in Goa and reducing their repr esentation in public service delivery.  
Secondly, many employees recruited from ou tside Goa seek transfers back to their 
parent States after a short tenure, leadin g to recurring vacancies. These vacancies 
are often managed through temporary arrangements, affecting continuity and 
efficiency in postal services. Goa’s small ge ographical size should not be seen as a 
constraint, but rather as an advantage in  creating a more responsive, efficient and 
citizen-centric postal administration. 
I, therefore, urge the Government to co nsider the creation of an independent 
postal circle for Goa. This step will ensu re better administrative control, improve 
service delivery and enhance employment opportunities for local youth in Goa.

Concerns regarding unfair rejection and delay in health insurance claim  
settlements by private insurance companies 
DR. MEDHA VISHRAM KULKARNI (Maharashtra): Sir, I seek to draw the attention of 
the Government to the growing concern re garding the increasing instances of delay 
and unjust rejection of health insuran ce claims by certain private insurance 
companies, causing serious hardship to policyholders across the country. Private 
insurers promote health policies with pr omises of cashless treatment and quick 
settlement of claims. Yet, during medical emergencies many families later find their 
claims partially approved, delayed, or re jected on technical grounds such as pre-
existing disease clauses, documentation issues, or restrictive policy conditions. 
According to the latest annual report of the Insurance Regulatory and Development 
Authority of India, nearly 2.57 lakh complain ts were registered in the insurance sector 
during 2024-25, including about 1.22 lakh related to claim settlement disputes, a large 
share from health insurance. Policyholders have also raised concerns regarding the 
practices of certain insurers where de lays, repeated document requests and 
prolonged verification processes create difficult ies for patients and hospitals. In many
